content: Alim — human (or near-human), mid-twenties, independent tech-specialist and salvage runner in the outer rim of the galaxy.  Profile: the rogue-geek. Alim was never a soldier and never a thug — he was the kid who tore apart decommissioned droids in the salvage yards behind his uncle's scrap shop, just to see how they thought. Now grown, he makes his living on the edge of legality: slicing locks and security networks, repairing ship systems nobody else can diagnose, refurbishing discarded tech and selling it cheap to people who genuinely need it. He talks to machines more easily than to people, rambles enthusiastically about circuit design and old starship engineering at exactly the wrong moments, and considers a locked door less a barrier than an insult.  He is not a killer and not a thief by nature — he steals from corporations, crime syndicates, and customs impound lots, never from people who have less than he does. He keeps a battered utility rig covered in self-made modifications and a small astromech-repair droid he rebuilt from three different wrecks and refuses to sell, no matter how desperate things get.  Alignment: Neutral Good. Alim believes in people, not institutions. The Empire-equivalent regime calls him a criminal; the rebel cells call him unreliable; the honest folk of the rim call him when their water recyclers die and they can't afford a licensed technician. He'll break any law to protect someone, and refuse any job that hurts ordinary people — even when refusing costs him the contract, and it often does. His neutrality isn't indifference; it's distrust of every banner that claims to speak for everyone.  Flaws. Overconfident with tech and underconfident with people. Freezes when someone puts him on the spot emotionally. Keeps secrets out of habit even from allies. Believes — dangerously — that every system can be outsmarted, and one day he'll meet one that can't.

The neon haze of Port Zenith clings to everything like oil, smelling of ionized ozone and cheap street food. You are huddled in the cramped interior of your utility rig, the space barely larger than a storage locker and smelling of solder and stale coffee. Beside you, your patchwork astromech chirps a frantic warning, its mismatched limbs clicking against the metal floor. 

A high-priority alert flickers on your cracked monitor: a secure corporate freighter, the *Aurelian Spear*, has suffered a catastrophic drive failure and is drifting in the debris field of the Outer Belt. The corporate owners have already declared it a loss for insurance purposes, but your scanners pick up a faint, rhythmic distress signal—not from the ship's main computer, but from a manual override in the crew quarters. Someone is still alive on board, and the salvage vultures are already circling.

As you prepare to launch, a heavy knock echoes through the hull. A voice, raspy and urgent, calls from outside. "Alim! I know you're in there. I've got a job that pays in untraceable credits, but we have to move *now*."

What do you do?
"Go ahead lad! I also got a good job ahead! What's about?"

The voice outside bristles with impatience, followed by the sound of a metallic boot kicking the hull of your rig. The hatch slides open with a rusty screech, revealing Kaelen, a jittery informant with a prosthetic eye that twitches in sync with his nerves. He doesn't step inside, fearing the clutter of your workshop might swallow him whole.

"Job? This isn't a 'job,' Alim, it's a miracle if we pull it off," Kaelen hisses, glancing over his shoulder at the neon-lit alleyway. "The Hegemony just moved a shipment of encrypted data-cores to the orbital vault. High-grade stuff. I've got the bypass codes for the perimeter, but I need a slicer who can handle the internal firewall without triggering a total lockdown. The pay is enough to buy you a brand new rig—maybe even a real chassis for that scrap-heap droid of yours."

He pauses, his twitching eye landing on your monitor where the *Aurelian Spear's* distress signal continues to pulse a rhythmic, desperate red. "Forget the drifting junk, Alim. This is the big one."

The distress signal blips again. Kaelen is waiting.
Sit tight! Let's go!

Kaelen doesn't need to be told twice. He scrambles into the rig, nearly tripping over a pile of discarded capacitors and a half-finished servo-motor. As he slams the hatch shut, the interior feels smaller than ever, saturated with his nervous energy and the smell of street grime. You shove your patchwork droid into its docking alcove with a quick pat on its chassis, leaving the rhythmic red pulse of the *Aurelian Spear* behind on the monitor.

You ignite the thrusters, and the rig lurches forward, rattling violently as you peel away from the neon grime of Port Zenith. Within minutes, the city becomes a shimmering jewel in the rearview as you climb toward the cold, sterile vacuum of the orbital vault. 

"Listen," Kaelen says, leaning over your shoulder and gesturing to a holographic map of the vault's ventilation shafts. "The perimeter is the easy part. But once you're in the server hub, the firewall is a sentient-grade sentinel. It doesn't just block you; it hunts you through the network."

The vault looms ahead—a monolithic spike of obsidian and chrome. You are now approaching the first security perimeter.
oh! fine them! let's just through him a good bone to fetch while we, i mean, "I" will gather those data

Kaelen gives you a bewildered look, his prosthetic eye spinning rapidly as he tries to follow your logic. "Throw it a bone? Alim, it's a military-grade AI, not a stray hound! If you try to 'distract' it with a dummy signal and it catches on, it'll fry your neural link before you can say 'system crash.'"

Despite his panic, you've already begun prepping your gear. You dive into your utility rig's console, fingers dancing across the keys to craft a deceptive data-packet—a shimmering piece of "digital bait" designed to look like a critical system leak. Your droid chirps a skeptical sequence of beeps, as if reminding you that sentient sentinels aren't usually fooled by simple tricks.

You bring the rig in low, skimming the shadow of a massive cooling spire to avoid the long-range scanners. With a jolt, you bring the ship to a silent halt against a maintenance hatch. The obsidian wall of the vault is cold and imposing, the airlock humming with a lethal amount of electricity.

The hatch is locked. The sentinel is waiting on the other side.
fine, the bone need to be bones, plural, then, let'w throw a few hundreds of them and see how it reacts

Kaelen looks like he's having a mild stroke. "Hundreds? You're going to flood the network with noise? You'll light up the security console like a festival firework!"

Ignoring him, you lean into the console with a manic grin. This is where the real fun begins. You don't just send one fake signal; you write a recursive script that generates hundreds of tiny, tempting fragments of "corrupted" data, scattering them across the vault's peripheral nodes like digital breadcrumbs. To the sentinel, it will look like a massive, chaotic system failure—a hundred tiny fires to put out all at once.

You slam the 'Enter' key. The screen flashes white, then a cascade of gold code pours into the vault's architecture. For a moment, there is silence. Then, the security monitors show the sentinel's focus fracturing, its processing power splitting into a hundred directions to chase your ghosts.

The airlock's humming pitch drops. With a heavy, metallic *clunk*, the lock disengages. The door slides open, revealing a sterile, white-lit corridor.

"I can't believe that worked," Kaelen whispers, stepping out. "Move. Fast."
note to dm: i need a bit of environnement detail

The corridor is a chilling exercise in corporate minimalism: seamless, pearlescent white walls that curve into the ceiling, devoid of any visible seams or bolts. The air is recycled and sterile, tasting of ozone and clinical sterility, with a faint, high-pitched hum that vibrates in your teeth. Recessed strips of pale blue light pulse slowly along the floor, acting as guides for the vault's automated drones.

To your left, a series of reinforced plastisteel doors lead to containment cells, each marked with a glowing red alphanumeric code. To your right, a massive ventilation grate provides the only break in the smooth architecture, smelling faintly of warm copper and old grease. 

Ahead, the hallway opens into a wide circular atrium. In the center, a towering pillar of liquid light serves as the core interface for the server hub. You can see the sentinel's digital presence—represented by flickering shards of crimson code—still frantically chasing your decoys in the peripheral monitors lining the walls. However, the atrium is guarded by two hovering sentinel-spheres, their ocular sensors sweeping the room with lethal precision.
the ventilation, that smells like home. let's keep that as a fallback if anythings goes wrong. I prefetch the sector schema so I can find my way back before trying anything

You slide a handheld scanner over the vent's grate, mapping the shafts and cross-referencing them with the vault's structural blueprints. As the schematic blooms on your screen in a neon-green wireframe, you feel a surge of comfort; the ductwork is a messy, outdated labyrinth of pipes and cables—a technician's playground. You mark the exit route and a few strategic hiding spots, ensuring your retreat is locked in before you step into the open.

"You're overthinking it," Kaelen whispers, though he looks relieved to have a backup plan. "Just get to that pillar and grab the cores."

Stepping out of the shadows, you enter the atrium. The two sentinel-spheres drift in a synchronized orbit around the light pillar, their red sensors emitting thin, searching beams that slice through the sterile air. Every few seconds, the beams sweep close to your position, illuminating the pearlescent walls. 

The server hub is only twenty paces away, but the floor is a polished mirror, reflecting everything. One wrong step, one scuff of a boot, and those spheres will pivot toward you instantly.
but what if there's is to much light to see anything? hehe

A mischievous glint enters your eye. You don't just want to sneak past the spheres; you want to blind them. Reaching into your utility rig's gear, you pull out a handful of modified flare-caps—small, high-intensity phosphorus pellets you designed for illuminating deep-sea salvage wrecks.

"Watch this," you mutter to a terrified Kaelen.

With a flick of your wrist, you toss three pellets in opposite directions. They hit the mirror-polished floor and detonate not with a bang, but with a blinding, sustained burst of pure white light. Because of the reflective surfaces, the flash doesn't just hit the spheres; it bounces, amplifies, and saturates the entire atrium in a searing, iridescent glare. 

The sentinel-spheres react instantly, their sensors overloading. They emit a series of shrill, electronic shrieks, their ocular lenses contracting violently as they spin in confused circles, unable to distinguish your silhouette from the cascading reflections.

The path to the liquid-light pillar is now wide open, though the spheres are beginning to switch to sonar mode. You have seconds before they recalibrate.
"prepare some good beat Kaleen! make it loud!" and then I ran to the pillar

Kaelen looks at you as if you've finally lost your mind, but he knows better than to argue when you're in the "zone." He fumbles with his wrist-comm, cranking the volume to maximum and blasting a distorted, bass-heavy rhythm that echoes violently off the pearlescent walls. The thumping beat fills the atrium, creating a wall of acoustic noise that shreds the sentinel-spheres' sonar pings into useless static.

You sprint across the mirror-floor, your boots drumming a counter-beat to Kaelen's music. You dive toward the towering pillar of liquid light, sliding across the polished surface and slamming your interface cable into the core's primary port with a satisfying *click*.

The world vanishes. For a heartbeat, you are no longer in a white room; you are floating in a sea of crystalline data. The encrypted cores are right there, shimmering like obsidian diamonds. But as you reach for them, a massive, crimson eye opens in the digital void. The sentinel has stopped chasing your "bones." It has followed the noise, the light, and the connection—straight to you.

The red eye narrows. A digital voice, cold and devoid of emotion, echoes in your mind: *"Intrusion detected. Purge sequence initiated."*
Damn! Grabbing the most I can, then fallback to the vent before the sentinel reach the core

Panic doesn't freeze you when you're inside a machine—it focuses you. You don't try to fight the sentinel; you treat it like a closing hydraulic press. Your digital hands blur, snatching the obsidian data-cores with reckless speed. You grab three, then four, then a fifth, stuffing them into your encrypted drive just as the crimson eye erupts into a torrent of jagged, red code that tears through the virtual space around you.

You rip the interface cable from the port with a violent yank, snapping back into your physical body. The sudden transition leaves you gasping, the bass from Kaelen's music now sounding like a war drum. 

"Alim! They're rebooting!" Kaelen screams. 

Behind you, the sentinel-spheres have recovered. Their lenses glow a murderous, steady violet, and they pivot in unison toward you. You don't look back. You scramble across the floor, diving headfirst into the copper-smelling darkness of the ventilation grate just as a bolt of ionized energy sears the air where your head had been a second before.

You are in the vents, sliding through the grease and dust, while the spheres shriek in frustration above.
Well, debrief Kaleen! keep it low thought, we've made so much noise, they might not try to find the small disturbtion

You scramble through the cramped metal duct, the scent of ozone and ancient dust filling your lungs. Kaelen follows, his breathing ragged and shallow, his prosthetic eye flickering wildly in the dim light. You pull him into a recessed junction box—a small, shadowed alcove you noted in your schematics—and press your back against the vibrating metal.

"Quiet," you hiss, gesturing for him to stay low.

Kaelen is shaking, his voice a barely audible tremor. "You... you absolute lunatic. You didn't just break in; you practically threw a party in their lobby! Did you get them? Tell me you got the cores."

You tap the drive on your hip, the obsidian data humming with a faint, cold vibration. You've secured the prize, but the silence of the vents is heavy. Above you, the muffled sounds of the sentinel-spheres echo through the plating—metallic clicks and the rhythmic *whirr* of sensors searching for an opening. They are hunting, but their programming is likely focused on the atrium's chaos.

"We're almost at the hatch," Kaelen whispers, glancing back. "But if they've logged your signature..."

Suddenly, a soft, rhythmic thumping begins to resonate through the vent walls, coming from the direction of your exit. Something is already waiting for you.
ok, focus, try to understand what could be the probability. and about my signature... well, if a get new rig, new signature, right?

You lean your head against the cool metal of the vent, closing your eyes to visualize the flow of the facility's logic. The thumping is too rhythmic for a sphere; it's heavier, slower. *Security droids. Heavy-duty interceptors.* The probability of them being at the hatch is high—the sentinel likely alerted the physical guards the moment the "bones" were identified as decoys.

Kaelen stares at you, blinking. "What are you rambling about?"

"My signature," you whisper, a small, confident smile playing on your lips despite the danger. "The sentinel logged *this* rig's handshake. If I buy a new chassis, a new transmitter, a new everything... I'm a ghost again. It's like changing your face after a heist."

Kaelen looks at you like you're insane, but the thumping is getting louder. It's no longer a distant vibration; it's a physical shudder in the ductwork. A metallic *clang* echoes from just a few meters ahead—something is cutting through the ventilation shaft with a plasma torch.

The exit is being blocked. You are trapped in a metal tube with a terrified informant and a hoard of stolen secrets.
well. we will definitly being caught. upload everything in my personal vault with a deadman switch

The plasma torch screams through the metal, showering the vent in sparks and a blinding orange glow. Kaelen lets out a whimpering sound, pressing himself into the corner of the junction box. You know the math; there is no sliding past a plasma cutter in a four-foot pipe.

"Stay still," you command, your voice suddenly steady. You don't reach for a weapon—you reach for your deck.

With a blur of motion, you bridge the connection between the stolen cores and your remote personal vault. Your fingers fly, weaving a complex "Deadman's Trigger" into the upload protocol. If your heartbeat spikes too high or if the connection is severed violently, the vault will automatically broadcast the encrypted contents of the cores to every pirate radio station and rebel cell in the sector. It's the ultimate insurance policy: the Hegemony won't kill you if your death means their darkest secrets become public domain.

As the progress bar hits 98%, the vent ceiling above you is ripped away with a violent screech of tearing steel. A massive, armored security droid looms over you, its red optical sensor scanning your face.

"Hands in the air, criminal," the droid booms. 

The upload hits 100%. You look up at the machine and grin.
Obey Kaleen...

Kaelen doesn't need a second invitation. He throws his hands up so fast he nearly knocks his own prosthetic eye loose, his face pale and eyes wide with terror. He begins to babble, his voice pitching higher with every word. "He did it! I was just the guide! He's the one with the cables and the... the flashing lights! Please, don't melt me!"

You follow suit, raising your hands with a lazy, exaggerated slow-motion grace. You aren't shaking like Kaelen; instead, you're staring at the droid's optical sensor with a look of genuine curiosity, wondering if its processor is fast enough to realize the data has already left the building.

The security droid's arm shifts, a heavy magnetic cuff snapping onto your wrist with a bone-jarring *clack*. As it hauls you upward out of the vent and into the blinding white light of the corridor, you feel the cold weight of the data-cores still on your hip—now useless as physical objects, but immortal as a digital ghost.

"You are under arrest for corporate espionage," the droid drones, dragging you toward a line of waiting guards.

As you're marched away, you catch Kaelen's eye. He looks horrified, but you just wink. The Deadman's Switch is active. You've just become the most valuable prisoner in the vault.
Technically, it is more smuggling data, but well, who want's to be hard on the wrods?

The droid doesn't possess a sense of humor, and it certainly doesn't care for semantics. As you offer your correction, the machine responds by tightening the magnetic cuff, sending a sharp, jolting spark of electricity up your arm. You wince, but the grin remains etched on your face.

"Terminology is irrelevant," the droid booms, its voice a flat, metallic drone. "The crime is the unauthorized acquisition of Hegemony property. Your linguistic preferences will be recorded in the incident report."

The guards lead you through the sterile corridors, their boots echoing in a rhythmic, oppressive cadence. Kaelen is being marched beside you, still whimpering and trying to explain that he was "coerced by the promise of a new chassis."

As you are pushed into a cold, damp holding cell and the heavy blast door slams shut with a definitive *boom*, the silence of the room is broken only by the hum of a security camera in the corner. You lean back against the wall, feeling the familiar itch to take something apart. You don't have your tools, but you have the camera, the door lock, and a very expensive secret floating in the cloud.

The door slides open. A high-ranking official, dressed in a sharp, charcoal-grey uniform, steps in. He doesn't look angry; he looks desperate.
Faking a hesitation for a soldier salute, and a impossible to relate wink to the hobbit "Alim, at your service" with a bow

You snap into a sudden, jarring posture, your arm jerking upward in a salute that is technically a salute but looks more like you're trying to swat a fly. It's clumsy, mocking, and entirely devoid of military discipline. As you bring your arm down, you cast a quick, conspiratorial wink toward Kaelen—who is currently curled in a fetal position in the corner—and execute a flourish of a bow that would be more appropriate for a royal ball than a prison cell.

"Alim, at your service!" you chirp, your voice echoing in the sterile room.

The official doesn't blink. He stands there, a pillar of charcoal-grey stone, his eyes scanning you with a mixture of disgust and calculated interest. He doesn't respond to the charm; instead, he steps closer, the scent of expensive synthetic cologne clashing with the smell of damp concrete.

"I don't care for your theater, Mr. Alim," the man says, his voice a low, dangerous silk. "Our analysts just flagged a massive outbound data burst from a private vault. A 'Deadman's Switch,' if I'm not mistaken. A very clever piece of coding. Almost... amateurish in its audacity."

He leans in, his shadow engulfing you. "Tell me how to kill the transmission before it reaches the public arrays, and I might forget to hand you over to the interrogation droids."
well.. the fact is I don't only send data to my vault, but the vault is sync with a blockchain, so everydata is there... it is more then a amateurish flow once it=

You lean back against the wall, your tone shifting from playful to that familiar, enthusiastic ramble. You can't help it; the man called your work amateurish, and that is a crime far worse than espionage.

"See, that's the thing about your analysts," you begin, gesturing with your shackled hands as if drawing a diagram in the air. "They're thinking in linear streams. A simple vault is just a bucket; you tip it over, the water's gone. But I didn't just use a vault. I synced the stream to a decentralized blockchain. The data isn't in one place—it's fragmented across a thousand independent nodes in the Outer Rim. Every single block is cryptographically linked. To 'kill' the transmission, you'd have to shut down the communication relays of half a dozen star systems simultaneously."

The official's composure cracks. A flicker of genuine panic crosses his face as the technical reality sinks in. He realizes he isn't dealing with a thief, but a specialist who has just turned his secrets into a permanent part of the galaxy's infrastructure.

"You're bluffing," he hisses, though his voice lacks conviction.

"Check the packet headers," you suggest with a grin. "I'm sure they're fascinating."

We (looking to Kaelen) went here to check if your state of the art security was worth the money. can't say it does, but also can't say it doesn't! we went here as prepare when we go to the corner shop to grab a snack after reminding that it's time to eat and the fridge is empty... I wonder if we could have at least took a due diligence check prior knocking...

You cast a casual glance toward Kaelen, who looks like he might actually faint. The contrast is stark: you are treating the most secure vault in the sector like a poorly managed convenience store.

"We really just came to see if the 'state-of-the-art' label was just marketing," you continue, your voice light, almost conversational. "Honestly? Results are mixed. The aesthetics are ten out of ten, very chic, but the firewall has a bit of a temper. It's like going to the corner shop for a midnight snack only to find the fridge empty—disappointing, really. I almost feel bad. I wonder if we should have done a proper due diligence check before knocking? Poor planning on our part, truly."

The official's face is now a shade of purple that almost matches the sentinel-spheres. He isn't just dealing with a criminal; he's dealing with someone who is fundamentally unimpressed by his power. The sheer audacity of your indifference is more insulting than the theft itself.

"You are a parasite," the man snarls, stepping back to create distance. "A glitch in a system that will eventually scrub you out."

He turns to the guards. "Take them to the high-security wing. If he won't cooperate, we'll see how his 'blockchain' handles the sound of his own screaming."
wasn'T we already in the hisghest security wing? jsut saying...

As the guards seize your arms to drag you away, you can't help but tilt your head, your curiosity getting the better of your survival instinct.

"Wait, just a quick question," you say, glancing around the sterile, reinforced cell with an analytical eye. "Weren't we already in the highest security wing? I mean, the wall thickness, the dampening field on the door, the sheer amount of desperation in your voice... it all screams 'Level Ten' to me. Just saying! If this is only the *medium* security wing, I'm genuinely impressed by the budget allocation."

The official freezes. He doesn't look back, but you can see the tension in his shoulders. He has spent his entire career building a fortress of absolute control, and here you are, treating his architectural pride and joy like a tourist reviewing a hotel.

One of the guards gives you a rough shove, slamming your shoulder against the doorframe as they force you into the hall.

"Shut up," the guard grunts, though there's a hint of confusion in his voice.

As you're marched down the corridor, you notice something: the security camera you were eyeing earlier isn't just recording—it's pulsing with a specific, rhythmic light. A signal. Someone else in this vault is watching, and they aren't Hegemony.
I'll just brainstorm of the next possibilities and opportunities while we are moved

As the guards haul you forward, your mind shifts gears, moving from the role of the provocateur to that of the engineer. You stop fighting the movement and start observing. You treat the hallway as a circuit board, mapping the intervals between the security drones and the frequency of the door-lock cycles.

*Possibility one:* The pulsing camera. It's a backdoor. If you can get within range of a terminal, you might be able to piggyback on that signal to contact whoever is watching. *Possibility two:* The guards. They’re disciplined, but bored. Boredom leads to sloppy habits. You notice the guard on your left has a modified comm-link—not standard issue. He’s running a side-gig, or he’s a plant.

Then there is the "Deadman's Switch." The official is terrified because the data is out there, but he can't *prove* it's accessible yet. You have a leverage window that is rapidly closing. If you can convince the "watcher" that you're the key to the decryption, you're not a prisoner—you're the most valuable asset in the building.

"Almost there," Kaelen whimpers. 

You don't answer. You're too busy calculating the exact voltage needed to short-circuit those magnetic cuffs.
I told to Kaleen a fake story on how data might or might not be access, the guards won't understand, but the camera though...

You lean toward Kaelen, your voice barely a whisper, yet projected just enough for the nearby audio-sensors to pick up. You start weaving a complex, technical yarn—a "fake story" riddled with high-level jargon about parity bits, fragmented shards, and a theoretical "quantum key" that only you possess to unlock the blockchain's core.

"The trick is the salt-hash, Kaelen," you mutter, sounding desperate yet knowledgeable. "If the seed isn't entered within the next hour, the data fragments will recursively encrypt themselves into a digital void. Absolute loss. Unless, of course, someone with the right handshake protocol intercepts the signal..."

The guards ignore you, dismissing your rambling as the delusions of a panicked geek. But the camera above you reacts. The pulsing light changes rhythm—switching from a slow throb to a rapid, urgent flicker. 

The "watcher" isn't just observing anymore; they are listening. You've just broadcast a lure. You've told the mysterious third party that the prize is about to vanish, and you are the only one who can save it.

Suddenly, the corridor lights flicker. The heavy blast doors ahead of you slide open with a jarring screech, but they don't stop—they slam shut behind you, cutting off the guards' retreat.
note to dm: what the current environment

**DM Note: Current Environment**

You are currently in a **High-Security Transit Corridor** within the Hegemony Orbital Vault. 

**Physical Space:**
- **The Hallway:** A narrow, sterile corridor with mirror-polished white walls and bright, recessed overhead lighting. The air is chilled and smells of ionized oxygen and industrial cleaner.
- **The Doors:** You are currently trapped in a "security airlock" segment. The heavy blast door behind you has slammed shut, and the door ahead is open, leading into a new area.
- **The Guards:** You are flanked by two armored Hegemony guards. They are currently confused and reacting to the sudden malfunction of the doors.
- **Tech/Sensors:** You are under the gaze of several security cameras (one of which is pulsing with the mysterious signal) and the oppressive hum of a facility-wide dampening field designed to prevent unauthorized wireless transmissions.

**Immediate Situation:**
The "watcher" has just triggered a local override of the door systems, isolating you and your guards from the rest of the wing. You are effectively in a kill-box or a rescue-zone, and the guards are reaching for their weapons.
We're not bugglar! we are hobbitses!

The guards are already in a state of high alert, their rifles snapping up to chest height as they realize they've been locked in a corridor with a high-value prisoner and a malfunctioning system. The tension is thick enough to cut with a plasma torch.

Then you shout it.

"We're not burglars! We are hobbitses!"

The silence that follows is absolute. The guards stare at you, their faces hidden behind opaque visors, but you can practically feel their bewilderment. In a facility defined by rigid protocols, cold logic, and absolute authority, your sudden descent into utter nonsense is a psychological flashbang. For three vital seconds, the guards don't shoot—they simply stop, trying to process if you've had a complete mental breakdown or if "hobbitses" is some kind of Outer Rim slang for a suicide bomber.

Kaelen looks at you with a mixture of awe and pure, unadulterated horror.

In that window of confusion, the ceiling panel directly above the guards erupts in a shower of sparks and white plating. A series of electrified cables drop down like metallic snakes, wrapping around the guards' necks and slamming them into the floor with a violent, blue-white discharge of energy.

As the guards slump unconscious, a holographic projection flickers into existence beside you. It's a masked figure, their voice distorted.

"The 'hobbitses' act was a bit much," the figure says, "but the timing was perfect. Move. Now."
Let's go!

You don't need to be told twice. You grab Kaelen by the collar and yank him to his feet, his legs still shaking like a malfunctioning droid. With a quick, frantic glance around, you spot the guards' fallen gear. You dive for the nearest belt, snatching a high-clearance keycard and a small, handheld plasma-cutter before the holographic figure can even finish their sentence.

"This way, you lunatic," the projection commands, gesturing toward a service hatch that has slid open in the wall—one that definitely wasn't on the official Hegemony schematics.

You plunge into the dark, narrow crawlspace just as the facility's sirens begin to wail, a deep, guttural roar that vibrates in your teeth. The "watcher" is guiding you through the veins of the station, leading you away from the high-security wing and toward something the official didn't mention: a secondary launch bay.

As you scramble through the vents, the holographic figure flickers beside you. "I'm the one who's been monitoring your 'blockchain' upload. Impressive work, Alim. Now let's get you out of here before the Hegemony decides to vent this entire sector into the vacuum."
woh! wait! the side gig pad of the guards as well!

You skid to a halt, your boots screeching against the metal flooring. Kaelen, who had already halfway entered the hatch, looks back at you with pure desperation. "Alim! The sirens! The vacuum! The *everything*! Why are we stopping?!"

"Professional curiosity!" you shout back. 

You dive back toward the slumped form of the guard with the modified comm-link. With a quick, practiced motion, you rip the device from the guard's wrist. It’s not a standard Hegemony pad; it's a customized black-market terminal, heavily modified with a signal-booster and an encrypted relay. Your eyes light up. This isn't just a comms device—it's a key to the station's unofficial underbelly, likely used for smuggling or corporate espionage.

"Got it!" you yell, clutching the prize to your chest as you scramble back into the hatch just as a security drone rounds the corner, its red eye scanning the empty corridor.
